Sumner presented petition from
81,215 citizens, praying for the abolition
of slavery.
On motion of Sherman the Senate
took up the substitute for prohibiting the
speculation in gold and exchange.

this bill was to prevent gambling in gold.

bill.

the committee on Invalid Pensions, re-
ported a bill, which was passed, supple-
mentary to the Law of So
Beaman, of Mich., from the Conference
Committee on the disagreeing amend-
ment to the bill providing a temporary
government for the territory of Montana,
made a report recommending concur-
rence to the Senate amendment, strik-
ing out the qualification of white voters
and substituting every male citizen of the
United States, and those who have de-
clared their intention to become such.

Holman moved to lay the report on
the table. Lost. Go to Go.

port, so to so.

to its amendment.

and ask another committee of confer-
ence.

lowing instructions: And that the Com-
mittee on Conference agree to no vote
which authorizes none others to vote
than free white citizens and those who
have declared their intention to become
such. The question was taken on these
instructions, and they were agreed to—
yeas, nays 81.

tee of Conference was then adopted, with
instructions as above.

unemployed Generals was postponed ten
days.

Washington, June 25th.
To General Dix:
The following dispatch has just been
received from Gen. Hirst.

I have the honor to report our expedition has been entirely successful in besieging great injury on the enemy and winning victories in every engagement. A Letter to the Editor.

Mr. Jno. A. Nye writes a long letter to the Denver Messenger, which published a copy. Mr. Nye is mad and says he has lost his loading up near the Blue at the time of the Indian scare, and abandoned it there. We are told part of it was burned up and part of it was carried away. Mr. Nye grows very angry in his letter and writes as follows:

"But the Kansas militia who came on the road, as if there was NO danger, ostensibly to fight the Indians and protect the road, disclosed their real purpose, showed out their real nature, making issue as they were in an enemy's country, by carrying off all they could pick at their horses. This took all kinds of valuable goods and implements, and destroyed and left to spoil much that, but for them, would not have been much lost. I do speak of things that I know, and that I have felt, have seen. Horses loaded down with sacks of money, wrenches, and the shoes, strings of boots and dresses, enough to make one endorse a possible question that such men are not even the peers of those who sacked Lawrence, or who led the Indians in this bloody work. If any Christian should pray that lightning should strike a man who will ever travel by way of Marysville to or from Colorado again, hundreds of those who have suffered, will say Amen."

Now Mr. Nye, you go too fast. Just retain your linen and keep the fever down. You have said some pretty hard things about Marysville and the Kansas militia and without just cause. Nobody doubts but you are a bold brave man and have been greatly outraged. But if you live a thousand years and find out more of the facts of the case you will see how foolish the letter is. Come to Marysville, sir, and enquire after your property. Nobody will hurt you; but on the other hand the citizens will render you all the assistance and information possible to recover anything that may belong to you or that any other gentleman may have lost upon the road. We are earnest and politely ask you to come, and take our word for it no one will or wishes to harm you. We recently learned where there are some valuable goods taken from up the road, but they are not in this section of country, neither were they taken by the militia. We will give you information about this or any other property that may come to our knowledge.

The militia companies from Marysville took no property at all that was abandoned by freighters. A few dollars worth, and only a few dollars worth, was taken BY some other companies of militia, but it was not taken with the intention of stealing, but more for the purpose of saving it; and if Mr. Nye or any other man who has lost property that is in this section and will come after it, they can get it.

er in the Yankee boat. The Albemarle's

ship, but they could see nothing of the en-

Captain in command, surrendered, torpedo
boat and all.

The President of the U. S. has issued his
congratulations to the people, asking them
one and all join in giving thanks to their
homes and to their churches for the good
fortune which has attended the armies of
the nation within the last week. His con-
gratulations are couched in moderate and
thankful and temperate words—enough to
show that he feels deeply that we have
great cause to be truly grateful for this
large measure of success accorded to us, yet
enough to indicate also that he recognizes
that we have still persistent and strug-
gling and fierce foe to deal with.


The tone of our best exchanges is in
unison with the President's message to the
country. There is no irrational exultation
over exaggerated results. Indeed repres-
sion marks the comments of the leading
papers. All feel that decided advantages
have been won, but won at great cost and
after the fiercest and most deadly and most
protracted struggle of the war. Hence cool
and intelligent writers are well disposed
to view the remaining situation with auxi-
liary as well as with hope.


We believe now that Grant has made his
position South of the Rappahannock secure
against any possible contingency. He is
rapidly establishing a new base, one
that we have fought for twice, and lost at
great sacrifices—viz. the Rappahannock
river at and below Fredericksburg.
This base is now established while our
trout extends twenty miles further on to-
ward, Richmond.
How long we are to remain thus con-
fronting Lee in the angle formed by the
North Anna river and the Fredericksburg
and Richmond railroad, is a problem to
which we have no key as yet. All the
news of yesterday goes to show that Gen.
Grant is not disposed to give Lee any time
to recuperate or firm up on the North
Anna. We have the superiority in numbers,
and the hero of Vicksburg lies the
man of all our generals who has evinced
that Napoleonic quality—the appreciation
of time.


The country will naturally be impatient
of delay. It is remembered that Lee
escaped his fate twice—once after the bat-
tle of Austerlitz and again after the battle
of Gettysburg, by delay. People cannot
help fearing that what has happened
twice may happen a third time, albeit
there is more confidence now than ever in
the man who leads our armies and in the
resources at his command.


The temptation to be first into Richmond
must be strong, as between Grant and
Butler. It is easy to see that the latter is
determined to plant his banner there, first,
of all, if possible. All honor to the man
who does it, say we, whatever else may be
said of him by loyal or disloyal. It will
be something to hoist in that long and de-
faultly held fountain head of the rebellion
the insulted and despised flag of the Re-
public.


We can all afford to possess our souls in
peace. Remember that this time a year
ago we were desponding and despondent
about matters in the Southwest; all the
copperheads were praying that it was an
absolute impossibility to reduce Vicks-
burg. Jeff. Davis had pronounced it im-
pregnable when he was there on tour of
inspection, and all his followers and sym-
pathizers, as well as many who were mis-
believed that Grant was simply wasting
precious lives, precious time and precious
treasure, in attempting to invest it. But
he did the work, and did it, too, with less
men and less resources than he now pos-
sesses. We have many fold more chances
certainties we should rather say, for the

mond than we had of Vicksburg, and de-
spite all rebel assertions or all veal-knee
croaking, we shall take Richmond speedily.
Let every Union man rest his faith abso-
lutely on this. The situation is ours, if
men are ours, the resources are ours, and
the cause is ours. This rebellion is near-
ly at its last gasp.

To the Editors of the Enquirer:


Columbia, S. C., 3d March, 1854.


Gentlemen: In your issues of the 23d and 30th inst. I observe a COMMUNICATION signed W. calculated to do great injustice not only to myself, which is of secondary importance, but to the brave and loyal people OF New Orleans. The writer asserts that Gen. Lowell has made the "calculation declared that his abandonment OF New Orleans "was made at the urgent solicitation of the people and the authorities of the city." In this assertion he is altogether in error. Lowell has never made any such declaration. There is no such reason given, either in my official report, in my letters to the Adjutant General, or in my evidence before the Court of Inquiry. These documents are all on file in the War Department, and I presume that access can be had to them on proper application.


In my written report on file, there are several omissions in the printed copy. The following reasons are assigned for the evacuation OF the city, viz: "I adopted this course, etc., (withdrew the troops), recognizing the perfect absurdity of confronting mere than a hundred guns aboard of the largest caliber, well manned and served, looking down upon the CITY, with less than ten thousand militia, mostly armed with indifferent shot and guns. It would, in my judgment, have been a wanton and criminal waste OF life of women and children, without the most remote possibility of any good results, as the enemy had only one of his ships, Keaner, to command the Jackson Railroad, and he could have reduced the city TO ashes at his leisure, without our being able to make any resistance whatever; or, with no one firing a shot, he could have starved the CITY into a surrender in less than three weeks, as there was not more than eighteen DAYS food on hand for the population, from which MY troops were almost entirely drawn."


Furthermore, it is stated that this course, which I had already given as the result of "my own judgment," was in compliance with the openly expressed opinion of all the prominent citizens around me, that it would be an useless waste of blood, without being productive of any beneficial results to the cause; for the troops to remain. In my testimony, given under oath before the Court of Inquiry, the reason for the evacuation (which was entirely of a military nature) is fully stated, and in them no allusion whatever is made to the people of New Orleans. I spoke to the mayor, several members of the city council and many prominent citizens on the subject, and this none seemed unwilling to undergo any danger, if by so doing they could arrive at favorable results; yet all, without exception, under the circumstances opposed of and advised the withdrawal of the troops.


The EVIDENT intention, both in the report and in the testimony, was to convey the idea that the city was evacuated for careful controlling military reasons, which alone are assigned, and that this step was taken with the concurrence and approval OF the principal citizens I saw, and that the authorities recognizing that any attempt at further resistance under the circumstances, would have been a further sacrifice of life and property. Such, at least, was my intention, and if there is any ambiguity in the wording of my report, which I cannot discover, I now reiterate that intention most fully and unequivocally.


The portion of the report which relates to the interviews, i.e., relative to my return to the city after the evacuation, is entirely another matter and has no bearing upon it. The question there was, not whether the city could be evacuated, for that had been already done, but whether I should return with the troops and in connection with the other citizens undertake a desperate enterprise. I had understood that a portion of the authorities and some citizens, who had expressed their approval OF my course in evacuating the city, were IN favor of this enterprise, and that if the troops were present they would undertake it. I, therefore, returned to New Orleans and offered to assist in the enterprise although MY advice was against it. I found no person of authority or influence in favor of it, they being generally OF the same opinion as on the day of evacuation and they discountenanced it. I was willing to undertake the matter, although advising against it, principally because my troops were almost entirely composed OF citizens of New Orleans, enrolled for local defence, and if they were determined to expose themselves, their families and property in such a desperate resistance, I was resolved, as their leader, not to abandon them. It is distinctly stated in my Report that "such a step would be entirely indefensible from a military point of view" and that the only palliation for such an act would be that it would give unmistakable evidence to the world that our people were deadly earnest;" but it is still an open question whether the moral effect of such a step would not have a tendency to lose life in the end, by giving our enemies a bloody foretaste of the task before them.

message" We have already shown

al under the State laws was to wide in

not within the province of one nation to
dictate TO another. No nation has a

ploy in its armies certain class of peo
pie. The composition OF armies is a

thoriles of the nation itself. If the

The working men and women at the North. During the week before last they held large demonstrations in New York, gotten up under the auspices of the Working Womens Protective Union. Knoxville, Tenn., Sept. 5, 1864.
The following Official telegram from General Gillem
was received this evening.--


BULLS GAP, Tenn., Sept. 4, 1864.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 6, 8:10 P.M.
For General JOHN A. DIX, New York.


despatch from General Gillem just received, gives
statement from the Richmond Examiner this morning
Morgan surprised and killed, and his STAFF
captured, at Greenville, Tenn., yesterday.


An unofficial despatch by this department this
morning from Lexington states that General Gillem had
only reported the surprise and defeat of Morgan at
Greenville; that John Morgan killed and his staff
captured; from fifty to hundred rebels killed, seventy
prisoners taken and guns captured. This report being
confirmed by the Richmond Examiner, there is room
to doubt its truth.


EDWIN M. STANTON, Secretary of War.
Sketch OF the Rebel General Morgan.
Brigadier General John H. Morgan is the eldest of six
brothers, all of whom have been in the rebel service.
Born at Lexington, Ky., about the year 1826, and is
the manufacturer of jeans in that neighborhood.
He received his education also, in that State; he raised
a company of Kentuckians for the Mexican war, but
failed to get service. After that had ended he
entered the jean business and married Miss Re-
becca Bruce, since dead. When the rebellion broke out
and his band of guerrillas in Kentucky he was at
that time a captain of the Lexington Rifles militia
organization and went with them into the seceded States.
From his early youth he had been a daring, reckless
rider, and well suited to the line or the vice he
had chosen. He first began his operations in Missouri,
where his name at last became terror and bug-
bear. He then moved into Kentucky, operated
near Bacon creek, harassed the Union army
of the Ohio during their advance towards NASHVILLE. He
had attached to his staff a telegraph operator named
Ellsworth, who before despatches sent cypher,
would take the orders of the Union from the
wires and thus defeat all plans of Union operations, the
rebels being ready to meet them. For his skill he
appointed colonel and afterwards brigadier general,
in the rebel army of the rebel States. During November
1862 he was acting with Bragg in Tennessee,
and there married Miss Ready, who had
retreated to Louisville for that purpose. He con-
tinued his operations south of the Cumberland river
until July 1862 when he made his dash in or through Ken-
tucky to Indiana and Ohio, which he and
his band captured and imprisoned. He dug his
way out of his cell on the night of November 11, 1862,
and, after many hazardous escapes, succeeded
in reaching the rebel lines late December. He
then set about raising command, under
orders from the rebel War Department of June
28, 1864; and during the summer of
the present year he was in the saddle, operating
in eastern Virginia and Eastern Kentucky. The states
bordering on the Ohio river fail men enough
to resist his advance, and as a result resulted in failure.
His command was the force attached to the cavalry
forces operating around Atlanta and served under
Wheeler during the recent raid upon Sherman's com-
munications. During this last raid he has lost many.
General Morgan reported to have been very KIND to
his prisoners and to have respected the law in
his treatment of the dead in forces that fell into his
hand. He is about six feet in height,
straight arrow and well proportioned. His hair
is light and curly, and he wore a heavy beard and
mustache, without side whiskers. His eyes are small
and gray and his complexion is fair.

An Act for the Incorporation of the Masonic Hall Annexation

a. Washington, District of Columbia.

b. 46 sess— as passed and approved in the Assembly of the Grand Masters of the Grand Chapter of the Grand Royal Arch Chapters of the United States; George W. Whiting, the Grand Consistory; L. Stevens.
II. Osiris Lodge of District No. 1; J. Gillian, of Washington and Aldwy, Me. No. 1; "Par Tulis" of Columbia; J. Smith of Columbia; Royal Arch Chapter, Ne. Is; W. Parkhurst, of Washington; II. Royal Arch Chapter, NJ. Is; James Stephens, of Mount Vernon Royal Arch Chapter, No. 90 c. y. Sssasbsry, of the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia; Joseph Nara, of Osiris Lodge, No. 1; J. Aeksr, of IsbaEOa Lodge, No. 1; J. KioRsan, of St. Justus Lodge, No. 3; J. N. Turton, of Hiram Lodge, No. 10; J. Fisher, of Saint John's Lodge, No. 11; L. G. Schimer, of NilcIGAl Lodge, No. 12; J. Yakiswick, of Washington Centennial Lodge, No. 14; J. G. McssuiFs, of B. FesseA Lodge, No. 15; J. L. Harvey, of Dawson Lodge, No. 16; J. W. Cray, of Harmony Lodge, No. 17; J. N. Hanson, of Acacia Lodge, No. 18; J. N. D. Larasr, of Lafayette Lodge, No. 19; of the Order of Free and Accepted Masons in the District of Columbia, and their Successors.

Be it enacted in the manner hereinafter declared: That the persons named and designated in this act are hereby incorporated and may lawfully associate and operate as the Masonic Hall Annexation Association of the District of Columbia, and by that name may have and use a corporate name, and may have and use a seal, and that for the purposes aforesaid, and to carry on and exercise all the powers and privileges incident to such a corporation.

Be it enacted that the said corporation shall have perpetual succession, and that the said corporation shall consist of the persons named in the first section of this act, and their successors.

Sec. 1. And it is hereby enacted, That within ninety days after the passage of this act, the persons named in this first section, or a majority of them, in case of failure or neglect to act, they hereby, the Masons shall cause books of subscription of the capital stock of the said corporation to be opened and kept in such place as may be appointed by the said corporation.

Sec. 2. And it is further enacted, That the stock of said corporation shall not exceed one thousand dollars; the stock shall be divided into shares of twenty dollars each; and each share shall be assessed as personal property, transferable in such manner as the constitution and bylaws of said association shall direct.

Sec. 3. And it is further enacted, That within ninety days after the passage of this act, the persons named in the first section, or a majority of them, in case of failure or neglect to act, they hereby, the Masons shall cause books of subscription of the capital stock of the said corporation to be opened and kept in such place as may be appointed by the said corporation. And all subscribers to said stock of the capital stock of the corporation shall be listed.

Sec. 4. And it is further enacted, That every subscriber shall pay at the time of subscribing each premium to the treasurer, and all subscribers to the treasurer shall be appointed of the corporation, and a majority of them may be trustees of said corporation. The books of subscription—the capital stock of said corporation shall be closed, the corporation having held in the first section, the Masons of them, as is specified in this act. The trustees shall hold meetings within twenty days thereafter, for the first meeting of the trustees held after the said corporation is organized. Each meeting shall be held ten days after, for the election of directors, which election shall be held for three years, and published daily in Washington City, by sufficient Masonic notice served on each trustee by the clerk or secretary of the corporation. And all meetings of the trustees shall consist of the holders of one vote.

Sec. 5. And it is further enacted, That the management and direction of the affairs of the corporation shall be invested in board of directors, consisting of members elected from the Masonic bodies named in the first section of this act, and the members hereinafter declared by the Masonic bodies they represent, who shall hold their office for one year, and all others duly elected and organized; and their places vacant upon the death of any of the said directors. The said directors shall elect from among themselves a president of the board, who shall be president of the corporation, and shall not be selected from among themselves. The directors assembled, who shall also be secretary of the corporation, and shall issue certificates, which shall give bonds with surety to said corporation, to such directors may require, for the faithful discharge of their functions. The treasurer shall from time to time for the transaction of business, and in such exercises, the board of directors, in the event of the death, resignation, or otherwise, of any director, it shall be necessary that they shall be filled by the remaining directors from among the corporation members in the first section of this act. Their duly elected appointed in the manner hereinafter declared by the Masonic bodies they represent.

Sec. 6. And it is further enacted, That the officers shall have full power to manage and direct such affairs as they may deem necessary and proper for the disposition and assets of the corporation, according to the charter and the laws of the United States and the ordinances of Washington City, and shall have power to issue such assessments as may be necessary for the trusts of the corporation in their opinion may require. And the said directors shall have power to regulate the payment of interest upon the bonds held by the holders, and shall have held dividends upon fixed and qualified terms.

Sec. 7. And it is further enacted, That each Masonic body of this association shall meet during the month of November, eighteen hundred and sixty-four, and annually thereafter, to meet and elect a ballot, and of its members, successor to the person then in office, representing a member of this corporation, whose annual term expires amongst those of which we have expired next thereafter; that said corporation shall forever consist of such corporation from each of the said Masonic bodies named for the first section of this act.

Sec. 8. And it is further enacted, That should any of the said several Masonic bodies named in the first section of this act surrender or cease to function, or from any cause cease to exist, and shall not be able to provide any representation to said corporation, shall the said corporation maintain its existence and rights of this association, be to any extent altered thereby, and this act shall remain in force.

Sec. 9. And it is further enacted, That any suit, complaint, or proceeding, whether civil or criminal, to be instituted in the District of Columbia may be brought with the consent of two-thirds of the officers named in the first section, their successors upon an equal footing with the several Masonic bodies named in the first section of this act.

Sec. 10. And it is further enacted, That this act may be repealed or amended by the rules of the Congress of the United States and the ordinances of Washington City.

Approved, April 15, 1864.
